normalized.governing_thought: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing, not store hours, to get close to 3.0%
executive_summary: Gross margin and e-commerce, not wages, explain nearly four-fifths of the fall in operating income – Operating income fell from $47.9M to $15.3M while sales grew 6% – 3.0% needs about $30M more a year; the FY2026 covenant needs $4.7M more

Fewer promotions, more private label and less shrink would win back about $17M of gross margin a year – 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money – Shrink is 3.1% of sales in the least-staffed stores, 2.3% in the best

Store hours should be moved, not cut, and the weakest stores exited as their leases end – An 8% hours cut could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving – Exiting the nine loss-making stores adds about $6.6M a year
E-commerce loses about $10M a year; the tested delivery fee cuts that by $2.8M and keeps the service – Each home delivery loses about $12, seven times a collected order

The plan gets to about 3.0% by FY2028 for $7.5M; its first two actions can clear the FY2026 covenant – Started at once, promotions and the fee lift FY2026 to about $23M – About $0.4M short of 3.0%; it also needs the 2027 wage rise absorbed

slides.title: Reversing the decline in operating margin
Key questions

claims.claim: How can Harlow lift its operating margin from 1.0% to at least 3.0% by FY2028, within $25M of one-time cost and with at least $20M of operating income in FY2026, and which actions should come first?
evidence: Decision maker: CEO, asking the board to approve the margin plan

Success criteria: Operating margin of at least 3.0% by FY2028; Operating income of at least $20M in FY2026 (lender covenant); At most $25M of one-time cost or capital over FY2026–FY2028; Delivery kept in some form; no closure of a store with a lease beyond 2027 without a board vote
Timing: Board meeting, February 2027
Out of scope: Closing the delivery service; New stores, acquisitions and refinancing; Sales growth from new formats

Sub-questions: 1 What caused the fall in operating margin since FY2023, and how large is the gap to close? 2 How much of the lost gross margin can promotions, private label and shrink win back? 3 Should Harlow cut store hours, and should it exit its weakest stores? 4 Does e-commerce make money, and how can Harlow keep delivery without draining the margin? 5 Which actions come first, and does the plan meet the target, the covenant and the capital limit?

slides.title: Executive summary

claims.claim: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing, not store hours, to get close to 3.0%
evidence: See executive_summary points 1–5 (p. 5–7, 9–16, 18–22, 24–30, 32–38)

slides.title: Where the margin went
Sales grew 6% in two years, but operating income fell by more than two-thirds to $15.3M

claims.claim: Sales rose in both years, adding $83M by FY2025
Operating income fell in both years, and faster in FY2025
evidence: Operating income, $M: FY2023 47.9; FY2024 33.4; FY2025 15.3
Operating margin fell from 3.37% to 1.02% of sales over the period
Operating income fell $18.1M in FY2025 alone

slides.title: Gross margin and e-commerce, not store labor, account for nearly four-fifths of the lost operating income

claims.claim: Wages are a small part of the story: 78.8% of the $35.4M shortfall comes from gross margin and e-commerce
evidence: Bridge, $M: FY2023 47.9; Sales growth +2.80; Gross margin rate −15.32; Store labor −4.50; Occupancy and energy −2.98; E-commerce fulfillment −12.60; FY2025 15.3
Gross margin rate: down from 26.0% to 25.0% of sales, through promotions and shrink
E-commerce: fulfillment net of fees rose from 0.4% to 1.2% of sales
Store labor: 13% of the shortfall, yet it is the only line the draft plan targets
Other SG&A: unchanged at 4.7% of sales
Sales growth: the FY2023 operating margin applied to the $83M of extra sales. Other SG&A moved by less than $0.1M and is not shown

slides.title: Reaching 3.0% by FY2028 takes about $30M more operating income a year, and the covenant needs $4.7M more in FY2026

claims.claim: $4.7M more needed in FY2026 to meet the lender's $20M covenant
evidence: FY2025: $15.3M, down $18.1M in one year
Another year like FY2025 would take operating income below zero
Must come from actions that pay inside the year

claims.claim: $29.8M more a year to reach the 3.0% target at FY2025 sales
evidence: About twice today's operating income
Within $25M of one-time cost or capital
Fewer stores lower the dollars needed

claims.claim: $14.5M a year: what management's 8% hours cut is expected to save
evidence: About 49% of the gap to 3.0%
Margin of 2.0% even if all of it holds
Aimed at labor, the smallest of the three causes

slides.title: Where the margin went
Gross margin offers the largest prize, through three moves: fewer promotions, more private label and less shrink

claims.claim: Promotions grew past the point where they pay, and the events that lose money can go first
evidence: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money after counting the extra units sold

claims.claim: Private label earns more on every dollar and answers ValuMart on price
evidence: 12 pp more gross margin on private label than on national brands

claims.claim: Shrink follows staffing, so it falls where receiving and produce work is protected
evidence: 3.1% shrink in the least-staffed quarter of stores, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: Sized on the following pages, the three moves are worth about $17M a year by FY2028

slides.title: 2a: The shift to promotions was the largest drag on gross margin, about four times what private label won back

claims.claim: Promotions, not prices, drained gross margin; $10.5M a year: what the shift to promotions costs at FY2025 sales
evidence: Gross-margin effect, pp: Promotional mix −0.7; Shrink −0.5; Private-label mix +0.18
Promoted sales earn 14 percentage points less, and their share rose by 5 percentage points
Shrink: up from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales
Private label: share up from 17.0% to 18.5%, at 12 percentage points more margin
The three drivers add up to the 1.02 percentage-point fall in the gross-margin rate

slides.title: 2a: Harlow pays more for promotions on two counts: 29% of sales are now promoted, and vendors fund less of each markdown

claims.claim: One sales dollar in four was promoted in FY2023; nearly three in ten by FY2025
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Harlow now pays 54% of each markdown itself, up from 45%
evidence: −9 pp
Vendor funding: FY2023 55%; FY2025 46%
Category managers raised promotional depth in FY2024–FY2025 "to defend traffic against ValuMart"; vendor funding for FY2024 is not in the briefing pack

slides.title: 2a: To pay for themselves, promotions would need about 3.5% more sales, more than twice the gain the category team cites

claims.claim: Promotions would need about 3.5% more sales to cover the margin given up
evidence: 5 pp more of sales on promotion × 14 pp less gross margin ÷ 20% contribution = 3.5%

claims.claim: The category team's evidence falls well short of that bar
evidence: Stores with the deepest promotions grew comparable sales 1.8% in FY2025, against 0.2% for the rest: a gap of 1.6 percentage points
That gap is a one-year correlation; it does not show that promotions caused it
Promoted sales earn less than the 20 cents a dollar used here, so the true bar is higher
41% of shoppers call Harlow more expensive, up from 33%: deeper promotions did not change price perception

slides.title: 2a: The threat promotions were meant to answer is local: stores near a new ValuMart lost 4.2% of comparable sales

claims.claim: Defend where ValuMart competes, cut elsewhere
evidence: Comparable sales FY2025: Within 3 miles of a new ValuMart −4.2%; Other Harlow stores +1.1%
11 stores have opened in Harlow trade areas since 2023
Why shoppers come: fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%) lead, so broad promotions buy little loyalty

claims.claim: Cut loss-making events away from ValuMart first; keep targeted price investment where it competes
evidence: The briefing pack does not give the number of Harlow stores within three miles of a ValuMart

slides.title: 2b: Keeping private label's current pace would lift its share to about 21% by FY2028, worth about $3.8M a year

claims.claim: Private label share to about 21% by FY2028, worth $3.8M a year
evidence: Private-label share: FY2023 17%; FY2024 17.7%; FY2025 18.5%; FY2028 plan 20.75%
18.5% + 2.2 pp (0.75 pp a year for 3 years) = 20.8%
2.25 pp of sales × 12 pp margin gap × $1,412M sales

claims.claim: The value answer that also pays
evidence: Each dollar moved from national brands earns 12 cents more gross margin
An own-brand price ladder answers the 41% who find Harlow expensive, without deeper promotions

slides.title: 2c: Shrink rises as staffing thins: the least-staffed stores lose 3.1% of sales, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: Thin staffing shows up as waste
evidence: Shrink by labor-hours quarter: Q1 3.1%; Q2 2.7%; Q3 2.4%; Q4 2.3%; Chain average 2.6%
Q1: store managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
Q3 to Q4: the extra hours buy only 0.1 percentage points less shrink, so Q4 stores can give hours up
Fresh and produce waste is 45% of shrink and receiving errors 20%
Chain: shrink rose from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales as hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0%

slides.title: 2c: Bringing the two least-staffed quarters of stores to the third quarter's shrink would save about $3.5M a year

claims.claim: Saving of about $3.5M a year
evidence: 1 pp excess shrink of Q1 (0.7 pp) and Q2 (0.3 pp) over Q3's 2.4% × 25% of chain sales in each quarter × $1,411.9M sales base after store exits = $3.5M

claims.claim: Hours move between stores; they are not added
evidence: Hours come from Q4 stores, where extra hours cut shrink the least
Theft, 35% of shrink, is assumed unchanged
Treats the pattern across store quarters as cause and effect; Q4 shrink may rise a little as hours leave
Chain shrink would fall from 2.6% to about 2.4%, still above FY2023's 2.1%

slides.title: Where the margin went
Store costs should be reshaped rather than cut, by redeploying hours and exiting the weakest stores as leases end

claims.claim: An 8% hours cut targets the smallest cause, and much of its saving would come back as shrink
evidence: 12.7% of the operating-income shortfall since FY2023 came from store labor

claims.claim: Six of the nine loss-making stores can close at lease end, with no board vote needed
evidence: 6 of the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA have leases ending by 2027

slides.title: 3a: Wages are not the main cause: fewer hours absorbed most of a 9% pay rise, and labor rose 0.3 percentage points

claims.claim: Fewer hours per sales dollar offset nearly three-quarters of the wage rise
evidence: 9.4% rise in average hourly wage: from $16.80 to $18.38
−5.98% change in labor hours per $1,000 of sales: from 7.02 to 6.60
0.3 pp rise in store labor as share of sales: from 11.8% to 12.1%
Total hours roughly flat while sales grew 6%

claims.claim: The 2027 minimum-wage rise of 4% needs the same productivity again

slides.title: 3a: An 8% hours cut could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink

claims.claim: Net saving of $4.5M before any lost sales
evidence: $14.5M (8% of $181.9M store labor) − $10.05M extra shrink = $4.5M
FY2023–25: hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0% and shrink rose 0.5 pp, about 0.08 for each 1% fewer hours
An 8% cut would add about 0.67 pp of shrink on FY2025 sales of $1,503M
Not counted: lost sales from checkout waits and stock-outs

claims.claim: Even if all of the $14.5M held, the margin would reach only about 2.0%

slides.title: 3b: Nine stores lose money at the four-wall level, and six can go without a board vote as leases end

claims.claim: Nine stores lose money at the four-wall level
evidence: 9 of 58 stores had negative four-wall EBITDA
$118M combined sales (7.9% of chain sales), four-wall EBITDA loss of $3.1M
25% of the sales would move to nearby Harlow stores, as in past closures

claims.claim: Letting the six leases run out costs nothing and needs no board vote
evidence: 6 of the nine have leases ending by 2027
The other three need a vote and $7.5M to exit

slides.title: 3b: Exiting the nine stores would add about $6.6M a year, and the six with expiring leases need no board vote

claims.claim: Exiting all nine adds $6.6M a year
evidence: $118M × 25% moved × 12% contribution + $3.1M EBITDA loss removed = $6.6M

claims.claim: Six exits need no board vote; the other three cost $7.5M
evidence: Six stores add about $4.4M a year, if the gain splits evenly by store
The other three add about $2.2M a year for a one-time $7.5M, a payback of about 3.4 years
Depreciation saved is not counted
Chain sales fall by about $88.5M

slides.title: Where the margin went
E-commerce can keep its delivery service, but only if delivery stops being subsidized

claims.claim: Counted in full, e-commerce loses money; the reported profit leaves out delivery and counts every sale as new
evidence: 30% of online spend is new to Harlow

claims.claim: Home delivery, not click-and-collect, causes most of the loss
evidence: $10.7 per delivered order: third-party delivery cost minus the fee collected

claims.claim: Repricing delivery as tested recovers part of the loss and keeps the service
evidence: $6.4 average fee per delivered order in the fee test, against $3.10 today

slides.title: 4a: E-commerce fulfillment cost more than tripled in two years, to $18.1M, the fastest-rising cost Harlow has

claims.claim: Growth came with the costliest kind of order
evidence: Fulfillment cost, $M: FY2023 5.2; FY2024 10.9; FY2025 18.1
Orders: 2.9 times as many as in FY2023, at a steady basket of about $96
Home delivery: up from 45% to 58% of orders
Gap per delivery widened from $9.50 to $10.70
Fulfillment cost per dollar of e-commerce sales, FY2025: 14.2%
E-commerce rose from 3.0% to 8.5% of sales

slides.title: 4a: Counted in full, e-commerce loses about $10M a year, because its new sales cover less than half of fulfillment

claims.claim: Contribution after fulfillment is −$10.4M
evidence: $127.8M e-commerce sales × 30% new (survey, n = 2,300) × 20% contribution − $18.1M fulfillment = −$10.4M
New sales cover 42% of fulfillment; home delivery carries about nine-tenths of the loss

claims.claim: Where data is missing, the estimate favors e-commerce
evidence: Store costs saved when an existing customer shops online are not counted
The 30% of new spend comes from customers' own answers and could be lower
Packaging and technology costs outside the fulfillment line are not counted

slides.title: 4a: The team's 6.1% profit comes from leaving out delivery and counting every online sale as new

claims.claim: The team's 6.1% profit comes from leaving out delivery and counting every online sale as new
evidence: Sales counted: team all sales as new; review only 30% new — largest correction
Third-party delivery: team left out; review included, $8.3M net in FY2025
Result FY2025: team 6.1% (about $7.8M); review loss of about $10.4M, 8% of e-commerce sales; a swing of nearly $18M

slides.title: 4b: Each home delivery loses about $12, more than seven times the loss on a click-and-collect order

claims.claim: Delivery, not online shopping, is the problem
evidence: Per delivered order: contribution $5.76; picking −$7.40; third-party delivery −$13.80; fee +$3.10; result −$12.34
7.5x the loss on a click-and-collect order
Click-and-collect loses about $1.64 an order
Delivered orders: 58% of orders but about nine-tenths of the e-commerce loss

slides.title: 4c: Customers accept a higher delivery fee: the test doubled the fee per delivery while e-commerce sales fell only 2%

claims.claim: Delivery stays, priced closer to what it costs
evidence: Fee test, 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025: fee $7.99 (from $4.99), free delivery from $100 (from $75)
$6.4 average fee per delivered order, up from $3.10 (2.1 times)
−9% delivered orders; +14% click-and-collect orders; −2% total e-commerce sales
Only 4 stores for 10 weeks: confirm in the rollout

slides.title: 4c: Rolled out to every store, the tested fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.8M a year

claims.claim: Gain of $2.8M a year
evidence: $18.1M − $15.1M − $0.2M contribution lost = $2.8M
Costs per order stay at FY2025 levels: $7.40 to pick, $13.80 to deliver

claims.claim: The fee is a first step; the delivery contract matters as much
evidence: Every $1 off the delivery rate at renewal adds about $0.7M a year; the proposed 3% rise would cost about $0.3M
E-commerce would still lose about $7.6M a year

slides.title: Where the margin went
Together the actions would lift operating income from $15.3M to about $42M a year by FY2028

claims.claim: Operating income to $42.00M FY2028 run rate
evidence: $15.3M + $17.2M gross margin + $2.8M delivery fee + $6.6M store exits = $42.00M
Gross margin: promotions $9.9M, private label $3.8M, shrink $3.5M, on sales of $1,412M
One-time cost: $7.5M to exit three leases, within the $25M limit
Store labor held at 12.1% of sales: scheduling must absorb the 2027 minimum-wage rise of 4%
Not counted: sales growth, a lower delivery rate at renewal, and depreciation saved
On the smaller sales base, 3.0% means about $42.4M of operating income

slides.title: The plan returns the operating margin to about 3.0% by FY2028, with almost no cushion

claims.claim: Operating margin about 2.97% by FY2028
evidence: Operating margin: FY2023 3.37%; FY2024 2.27%; FY2025 1.02%; FY2028 plan 2.97%
Gap: about $0.4M below 3.0%
2027 wage rise: if scheduling does not absorb it, about 2.5%

claims.claim: Treat the delivery re-tender as part of the plan, not an upside
evidence: $0.5 rate cut closes the gap: $0.4M ÷ about 703 thousand delivered orders
Each $1 off the rate adds $0.7M a year

slides.title: The recommended plan beats the labor-cut plan on margin, on the covenant and on risk to shoppers

claims.claim: Only the plan reaches the target
evidence: Draft: about 2.0% if full $14.5M holds; nearer 1.3% if shrink rises; plan: about 3.0% (2.97%)

claims.claim: Ours clears $20M without a bet on shrink
evidence: Draft FY2026: $19.8M to $29.8M; plan: about $23M

claims.claim: Risk to shoppers smaller and targeted
evidence: Draft: fewer staff for fresh produce and checkouts; plan: fewer promotions, price investment kept near ValuMart

claims.claim: E-commerce: both keep delivery
evidence: Draft: frozen at loss of about $10M; plan: loss cut to about $7.6M

claims.claim: One-time cost within the limit
evidence: Draft: none; plan: $7.5M of the $25M limit

slides.title: Started at the beginning of FY2026, promotions and delivery pricing alone would lift operating income to about $23M

claims.claim: FY2026 operating income $23.4M
evidence: $15.3M + $5.3M half promotion reset (to 26.5% of sales) + $2.8M delivery fee = $23.4M
Headroom over the $20M covenant: about $3.4M

claims.claim: The covenant holds only if the FY2025 slide stops
evidence: A repeat of FY2025's $18.1M fall would breach the covenant
If FY2026 is the year ending January 2027, most of it has passed by the board meeting: start both actions now and agree the test with the lender

slides.title: Promotions and the delivery fee come first because they need no capital and add profit within FY2026

claims.claim: Approve the promotion reset and the fee now; the store vote and private label follow
evidence: Sequence FY2026–FY2028: Promotions — cut loss-making events, away from ValuMart first, back to 24%; Delivery — tested fee chain-wide, re-tender contract; Shrink — move hours to receiving and produce; Private label — about 0.75 pp share a year; Store exits — six leases end, three after a board vote
Confirm the covenant test period with the CFO

slides.title: Five risks need an owner from the start, led by a loss of traffic to ValuMart

claims.claim: Five risks need an owner
evidence: ValuMart traffic (Chief merchant): largest risk; stores near a new ValuMart already lost 4.2% of comparable sales
2027 wage rise (COO): schedule to about 6.35 hours per $1,000 of sales
Delivery demand (E-commerce lead): steer to free click-and-collect
Delivery contract (CFO): re-tender before 3% rise
Store exits (Real estate): less than 25% of sales may move

slides.title: Six numbers will tell the board each quarter whether the plan is working

claims.claim: Six KPIs reported quarterly
evidence: Promotional sales 29% → 24% by FY2027
Shrink 2.6% → about 2.4% by FY2027
Average fee per delivered order $3.1 → $6.40 by FY2026
Private-label 18.5% → about 21% by FY2028
Store labor 12.1% → 12.1% or less every year
Operating income $15.3M → $20M or more FY2026; about $42M FY2028

slides.title: Four other routes were left out on purpose, two because they would make the problem worse
BACKUP: Four other routes were left out on purpose, two because they would make the problem worse

claims.claim: Four other routes were left out on purpose
evidence: Overhead: held at 4.7% of sales
Close delivery: family owners want delivery kept
Match ValuMart: deeper promotions already lost margin
Raise prices: 41% of shoppers already call Harlow more expensive, up from 33%

slides.title: BACKUP: As a share of sales, every line except other SG&A has moved against Harlow since FY2023

claims.claim: Every line except other SG&A has moved against Harlow
evidence: Occupancy and energy 5.8% / 5.9% / 6.00% (0.2 pp)
E-commerce fulfillment 0.4% / 0.7% / 1.2% (0.8 pp)

slides.title: BACKUP: Promotional mix, private label and shrink account for essentially all of the fall in the gross-margin rate

claims.claim: Three drivers account for the −1.02 pp fall
evidence: Promotional share 24% / 26.2% / 29% (−0.7 pp)
Private label 17% / 17.7% / 18.5% (0.2 pp)
Sum −1.02 pp; reported −1.02 pp
Vendor funding fell from 55% to 46% of markdowns; not a separate driver

slides.title: BACKUP: Absorbing the 2027 wage rise needs about 4% fewer hours per sales dollar, less than the drop since FY2023

claims.claim: Scheduling, not cuts, holds the labor line
evidence: −3.8% change needed
FY2023 to FY2025: stores cut 6.0% of hours per sales dollar
Upper bound: assumes the 4% rise lifts every wage

slides.title: BACKUP: Orders nearly tripled and home delivery's share rose while the fee collected per delivery fell

claims.claim: Orders nearly tripled and delivery share rose while fee fell
evidence: E-commerce share 3% / 5.6% / 8.5%
Delivered share 45% / 52% / 58%
Picking cost $7.2 / $7.3 / $7.4

slides.title: BACKUP: Picking, delivery and fees rebuild the $18.1M fulfillment cost, so the order data can be trusted

claims.claim: Fulfillment cost rebuilds to $18.1M
evidence: Delivered orders 771.98k; click-and-collect 559.02k
Picking $9.8M; delivery $10.7M; fees $2.4M
Fulfillment net $18.1M; Table 1 reports $18.1M

claims.claim: Eight planning assumptions
evidence: Promotions 24% (FY2023 level)
Private-label gain 0.8 pp a year
Shrink Q1 and Q2 2.4%

evidence: Plan as sized: about 2.97%

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Replace management's labor-cut plan with the recommended plan: reset promotions (cut loss-making events away from ValuMart first, back to 24% of sales), grow private label, move hours to cut shrink, roll out the tested delivery fee and re-tender the delivery contract, and exit the nine loss-making stores (six as leases end, three after a board vote). "Approve the promotion reset and the fee now; the store vote and private label follow." "Treat the delivery re-tender as part of the plan, not an upside."

alternatives_considered.option: Management's draft: cut store hours 8%, freeze e-commerce
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: targets the smallest cause; could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving through shrink; about 2.0% margin at best, nearer 1.3%; FY2026 $19.8M–$29.8M depending on shrink
Not in plan: it held at 4.7% of sales in FY2023–25, so it did not cause the decline
Not in plan: the family owners want delivery kept; repricing it is the route
Not in plan: deeper promotions already lost margin and did not change price perception
Not in plan: 41% of shoppers already call Harlow more expensive, up from 33%

alternatives_considered.option: Keep the three stores whose exit needs a board vote
alternatives_considered.treatment: Sensitivity: $2.2M of gain lost, margin about 2.76%; 'The vote matters'

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Eight planning assumptions for the CEO and CFO to confirm: promotions 24%, private-label gain 0.8 pp a year, Q1/Q2 shrink 2.4%, 25% sales per store quarter, 30% online spend new, 20% contribution per new dollar, 25% of sales kept from closed stores, 66.7% store gain from six leases
Planning assumptions chosen in this review (user unavailable to confirm)
All lever sizes use FY2025 prices, volumes and cost rates; the 3.0% target is measured on the sales left after the store exits and the fee change
Plan is about $0.4M short of 3.0% with almost no cushion; needs the 2027 wage rise absorbed (else about 2.49%)
Promotions delivering half would leave margin at about 2.62%
Comp-sales gap from deep promotions is a one-year correlation, not causation
Number of Harlow stores within three miles of a ValuMart not in briefing pack
Shrink saving treats the pattern across store quarters as cause and effect; theft assumed unchanged; Q4 shrink may rise a little
Hours-cut shrink effect is an upper bound; lost sales not counted
30% new online spend comes from customers' own answers and could be lower; some e-commerce costs/savings not counted
Fee test only 4 stores for 10 weeks: confirm in the rollout
Covenant holds only if the FY2025 slide stops; confirm the covenant test period with the CFO/lender
Store exit gain uses four-wall EBITDA; depreciation saved not counted; risk that less than 25% of sales moves
Five risks: ValuMart traffic, 2027 wage rise, delivery demand, delivery contract, store exits
next_steps: Start the promotion reset: stop repeating loss-making events, beginning away from ValuMart — Chief merchant — Now
Roll out the tested $7.99 delivery fee and $100 free-delivery threshold to every store — E-commerce lead — Within a month
Re-tender the delivery contract and confirm with the lender which months the FY2026 covenant covers — CFO — Now, before renewal
Replace the 8% hours cut with a move of hours to receiving and produce in Q1 and Q2 stores — COO — First quarter
Let the six leases lapse and put the other three exits to a board vote — CEO with the board — February 2027 board
